arml-2012-power-01a.prompt:
*(Power Question 2012: Cops and Robbers.)* A **map** $M$ is a set of hideouts, some pairs of which are adjacent (joined by an edge); every hideout is adjacent to at least one other. A Robber hides in one hideout, and **each night he must move along an edge to an adjacent hideout**. Every day, each Cop searches one hideout: if the Robber is there he is caught; otherwise the Cops learn nothing except that he was not in the hideouts searched. Cops are not constrained by edges: a Cop may search any hideout on any day, the same hideout on consecutive days, and several Cops may search different hideouts on the same day. $h(M)$ is the number of hideouts. The **Cop number** $C(M)$ is the minimum number of Cops required to guarantee that the Robber is caught.

Consider the hideout map $M$ shown: a central hideout $A$ adjacent to each of $B_1,\dots,B_6$, with no other edges. Show that one Cop can always catch the Robber.
arml-2012-power-01a.reviewNote: The book omits the opening paragraph of this Power Question (the rule that the Robber must move to an adjacent hideout every night); the setup in the prompt was reconstructed from the official solutions.

For $c\ge C(M)$ Cops, the **capture time** $D(M,c)$ is the minimum number of days required to guarantee a capture using $c$ Cops.

A **path** on $n$ hideouts, $\mathcal P_n$, consists of hideouts $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n$ with $A_i$ adjacent to $A_{i+1}$ for $1\le i<n$ and no other edges (the figure shows $\mathcal P_3$ through $\mathcal P_6$). Show that $D(\mathcal P_n,1)\le 2n$ for $n\ge3$.
arml-2012-power-03.answer: Sweep $A_2,A_3,\dots,A_{n-1}$ and then back $A_{n-1},\dots,A_2$; parity of the Robber's index minus the Cop's index shows capture within $2n-4$ days.

A **cycle** on $n$ hideouts, $\mathcal C_n$, consists of hideouts $A_1,\dots,A_n$ in a loop ($A_i$ adjacent to $A_{i+1}$, $A_n$ adjacent to $A_1$), and $C(\mathcal C_n)=2$. Show that $D(\mathcal C_n,2)<\frac{3n}{2}$ for $n\ge3$.
arml-2012-power-04b.answer: Cop 1 stays at $A_1$ while Cop 2 sweeps $A_2,\dots,A_n$ ($n-1$ days); a surviving Robber has the wrong parity, so after a one-day parity adjustment the two Cops close in from both ends ("pincers"): at most $\frac{3n-1}2$ days.

A map is **bipartite** if its hideouts can be partitioned into two disjoint sets $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ such that each hideout in $\mathcal A$ is adjacent only to hideouts in $\mathcal B$, and each hideout in $\mathcal B$ is adjacent only to hideouts in $\mathcal A$. Prove that if $M$ is bipartite with $n$ hideouts, then $C(M)\le n/2$.
arml-2012-power-07a.answer: Put Cops on the smaller side for two consecutive days.

A map is **bipartite** if its hideouts can be partitioned into two disjoint sets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ such that every edge joins a hideout of $\mathcal A$ to a hideout of $\mathcal B$; for such maps $C(M)\le n/2$ ($n$ = number of hideouts). Prove that $C(M)\le n/2$ for any map $M$ with the property that, for all hideouts $H_1$ and $H_2$, either all paths from $H_1$ to $H_2$ contain an odd number of edges, or all paths from $H_1$ to $H_2$ contain an even number of edges.
arml-2012-power-07b.answer: The condition makes $M$ bipartite: colour each hideout by the parity of the length of any path to a fixed base hideout (one base per connected piece).

A map $M$ with $n$ hideouts is called **$k$-perfect** if its set of hideouts can be partitioned into equal-sized subsets $\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2,\dots,\mathcal A_k$ such that for any $j$, the hideouts of $\mathcal A_j$ are only adjacent to hideouts in $\mathcal A_{j+1}$ or $\mathcal A_{j-1}$ (indices mod $k$: hideouts of $\mathcal A_1$ may be adjacent to hideouts of $\mathcal A_k$). Show that if $M$ is $k$-perfect, then $C(M)\le\frac{2n}{k}$.

(Earlier in this Power Question it was shown that two Cops can always catch the Robber on the cycle $\mathcal C_k$, $k\ge3$: one Cop always searches one hideout while the other sweeps the remaining path there and back.)
arml-2012-power-08.answer: The Robber's block index performs a walk on the cycle $\mathcal C_k$; two teams of $n/k$ Cops, each searching a whole block, imitate the two-Cop strategy on $\mathcal C_k$.
